blocks.x: Okay, Al, this is the first reel. It's going.
Okay, thanks. You're welcome. I'm sneaking out.
Okay.

Al, I'd like to ask you a question that interests me very much. What kind of a feeling do you get when you listen to, for instance, Big Spiderman solo? What kind of emotional fulfillment does that represent? What kind of people seem to be attracted to that kind of sound?

Well, I think that I understand the question. And, of course, as you understand, it's not my kind of people. That is, that I don't really respond emotionally to the Bix sound, although I understand it, I think. And I find it very interesting, but purely on an intellectual basis. But I don't have any visceral reaction to Bix. I feel that all of the arts, including music, is based on certain sound, on certain symbols that we are conditioned in such a way in our society so that we associate various symbols with various circumstances. I use as an illustration before we were on tape the idea of the C chord played on an organ. When you hear that chord played, even though it in itself is an abstraction, nevertheless, we all associate it almost automatically with the sound of a church. Because our conditioning has taught us to do that. And I believe that all of the sounds that we hear, or at least most of the sounds that we hear, we already have established associations with. Now, I also use the analogy of the typical romantic scene in a Hollywood color musical, in which you have a couple standing on a balcony in the moonlight, doing a song and dance, a romantic song, a stardust or something of that nature. And this is presented to us as representing the ideal in the man-woman relationship. Now, I have always felt like this is a fake ideal and that it has little or no relationship to the actual state of affairs as it exists between male and female in our society or indeed in the world. Now, I feel that the attitude that is expressed there, the ideals that are expressed there, are represented strongly in Bix's music and that he appeals largely to the same people who would respond to that kind of an image. It is also my conviction that in every society, virtually every point of view, every emotional attitude is expressed by some artist in every medium. And I further proposed that for practical purposes, such personalities as Edgar Guest and Guy Lombardo and Norman Rockwell were essentially the same, that they represented exactly the same point of view and appealed to the same people, though they worked in different idioms. Now, I know that in discussing with you that you frequently have made reference to the relationship between Bix and Gatsby as personalities.
Mm-hmm.
And while the analogies are clear enough there, we have to remember that Bix was a real personality and Gatsby is a fictional one.
Mm-hmm.

I would not make the same analogy between Bix and Fitzgerald, however, even though there were certain superficial similarities, but I don't think that anybody would contend that they were, for artistic purposes, the same. But I would draw your attention to the possibility of making such an analogy, for instance, between Bix and Thomas Wolfe, who fundamentally were from the same origins and developing the same kinds of attitudes and reactions, using similar symbols, although each in a different idiom.

Mm-hmm. Well, I have never, I have not read enough of Thomas Wolfe to know, but I know that you had mentioned that Bix's music conjures up to you the idea of the American dream, something about the American dream. That's right. That's right.
That's right. I mean, the real corner drugstore mom and apple pie attitudes, which were characteristic of his time in America. Now, the music signifies that to you.
The music signifies it. Not Bix's life.
That's right. The music, not the life. And that's where... Actually, I only knew anything at all about Bix's life very recently. I was never interested enough to find out.
Right.
All I knew was the music.

Okay. Now, let me ask, let me ask you this. If we make an analogy between his music and a kind of a romantic stock image, would it be fair to say that the romantic image of the two people on the balcony is pretty much a cliche dated image? In other words, we can look back at those 20 movies with Doris Day or whatever and say, well, this is a genre of the 20s. And we can sort of all partake in them and enjoy them because, well, we know that they're of a certain time and place and we enjoy it. But it's dated and a lot of it's corny.
See, I wish it were dated, John, but I really think that a large section of Americans still hold that image.

They probably do. But my point would be that it's been translated in some other way. Oh, very possible. Now, it may, I don't know what a modern analogy to that would be, but I think that all romanticism is taken out. For instance, sexual connotations in those movies were very, it was the dreamy, elusive, very suggestive, subtly suggestive sexuality. No overt sexuality at all. Very subtly suggestive. Oh, of course. Now, today you get the exact opposite. That's true. If there's any less subtle suggestiveness of sex as today in the movies, you know. So I'd say that that quality certainly is not present today. Another thing is that I think musically, in terms of Biggs' music, one of the remarkable things about his music, even when he's playing those solos in the Whiteman Orchestra, is that they are, they have so little of the quality of datedness, to my mind. They're so, they're so fresh and new.

Well, there's no question that Biggs was a highly competent artist. I have certainly never questioned that. The fact is that all I have said is that he does not have the emotional appeal for me because I really don't identify with his attitudes. But I certainly can't understand why many people will respond to what he's doing on a basis other than nostalgic.

Well, does he really have the, does he really, does his music really reflect those, those attitudes of that kind of image that you just described? Or is that something you may be reading into his music? Or that other people are doing?

If I were less sophisticated, I would say that I could be wrong in that. But actually I have investigated so much art, literature, and music. And even though, even though I am illiterate musically, I still have seen enough to satisfy me that this is the case. Because it seems to me that I am one of the people, few as they may be, who can broadly anticipate Biggs' playing. Because I felt that I understood him well enough to know where he would go. And this doesn't in any way detract from my estimate of his capacity because I can estimate Winging Manon too. But these are vastly different people. For instance, if I was going to make a direct contrast in jazz between two trumpet players from a standpoint of what they were saying, I would say that those would be the two.

Wouldn't the Whiteman Orchestra be a better representation of your kind of, your image of that foggy romanticism? And Biggs' playing within the Whiteman Orchestra was an antidote to that kind of saccharine?

That's a very good point. And I suppose there are degrees of that too. It may be that Biggs' presentation was more sophisticated than Whiteman's. But I still see it as part of the same package. Not only Biggs with Whiteman, but also Biggs with Goldkett or Biggs with Trumbauer. I don't, I can't, I can't find it in me to tar Whiteman with the same brush. I always heard it in Biggs' playing, except in the Wolverine days.

To my mind, the best of jazz or, if you want to call that music that he's playing jazz, which I think it was to a certain extent. I mean, you know, even within the New Orleans context. The best of it is, to my mind, is it has a very unsentimental quality to it. That is good jazz, it's not sentimental, it's not gimmicky, it doesn't have, it doesn't play cheap tricks on the emotions and things like that. Biggs' music, to me, does none of those things. It does not play cheap tricks on the emotions, but... I believe he was completely sincere. I think that the romantic hogwash of the 20s in the movies was kind of playing cheap tricks, just like any standard conventional idiom would. But I, you know, in other words, what I'm trying to suggest here is that... I just... You're saying Biggs is part of this, but...
Well, I think that Biggs presented all that without the cheap tricks. I believe...
What did he present?

Well, it is not possible for me to be able to translate into musical form these symbols. Not that I'm asserting that it can't be done, it's just that I'm not able to do it. But that whole romantic package is, to me, part and parcel of Biggs' music. Now, I believe that he may have been more sincere about it than Whiteman, but I believe that he was convinced. And I believe that he didn't need to use cheap tricks for it. I think it was part of his own personality. He was telling that story. He was painting that paradise.

Was it a... Is this part of the American Dream idea? Yeah, sure. What... How would you describe this American Dream thing? For instance, Gatsby's... The Great Gatsby, Fitzgerald's The Great Gatsby, always comes to mind in courses where themes of the American Dream come up. I know many courses that teachers, even on the high school level and even the college level, they title their courses, The American Dream. And, of course, since the Vietnam War, it's always been the American Dream gone sour, you know. And how elusive it is and how much it betrays us because we're always looking back. It's kind of a nostalgic thing and a self-defeating thing. And the image of Gatsby always comes up as this guy who's trying to grasp this platonic ideal in himself and in people outside of him. And it ends up in self-destruction.

Well, actually, that's because of the fact that the American Dream has very little to do with the realities of life in America. And that when the contradiction becomes apparent to the protagonist, the conflict as such is to make his existence untenable. However, there's also the consideration that in the early stages of the development of this country, for a long stretch of time, during the time when the economy and the political life of the nation was in its, in fact, ascendancy, which means merely that any man that was prepared to get out and do his work could enjoy the fruits of that work and that the frontier was available for everybody. Right. And so the individual capacity to go out and make one's way and solve one's problem and resolve one's life was available. Whereas by the time Bix came along, that circumstance had begun to draw to a close. But he had learned the ideal from his forebears and from his environment, which, after all, Davenport, Iowa, still remained in the cultural backwash of America. And it was still living on Chautauqua, so that the dream survived, but the reality died very briskly.
Would it be fair to say that Bix was living in a time in which the success myth was still very strong? Oh, certainly. And then he suffered from that?

No question about it. But the conflict began, I suppose, with him at that point where he was having his difficulties in trying to determine emotionally what constituted success. Fifty years earlier, it wouldn't have been a problem for him or anybody else, or at least for very few people. But the nature of success itself becomes more and more elusive in our society. Extrapolating it to today's circumstance, I would say there are very few people who are able to identify success. Extrapolating it to the world. And the contradictions caught up with Bix early because he was a creative artist. And because these problems bore in on him earlier than they did on his contemporaries.
But, in a sense, he, couldn't one say he didn't even care? That he just wanted to play his horn?

Well, you wouldn't be able to hear that in his horn. And you would have to know something about his life then. However, it seemed to me that he was constantly, he spent most of his life in search of approval. And he looked for the applause and he gloried in the response. He was not a congenital hermit by any means. And so, however, I am really never inclined to estimate a musician by his life, but only by his music. And what I hear is all I know.

Now, it's been said that, and I think Frank Power said this in a tape that he did in Bidebeck's life, that there was only one other musician that bare any resemblance to Bix Bidebeck. In the sense that both these musicians were victimized by the changing values of their time. And he mentions Charlie Parker. Now, I don't want to talk about, I don't want to bring up Charlie Parker. I'd rather talk about Bix Bidebeck. But, it's very interesting to me that he should bring up Charlie Parker in the relationship to Bix Bidebeck. Because I had decided before, even he had mentioned this, that these two figures, to me, were the ones that I was going to deal with. Because both of them resembled, in some way or another, something very close together. And I'm trying to figure out what it is. But I'm very interested in Frank Power's idea that Bidebeck was victimized by the changing social values of his time. And you're mentioning the shifting nature of the success myth and the elusive quality of the American dream. Did the depression, in a sense, would that be a good marking point for the failure of the American dream, in a sense that everything was confused now?

Well, it may have dramatized it to some extent, but I believe that the decline of the actualities behind the dream had already begun sometime earlier than that. I believe firmly that the American system has been in decline, demonstrably in decline, since the beginning of World War I. As far as the application of Charlie Parker, of course, I knew Charlie Parker and I didn't know Big Spider-Bank. However, it's fair to say that I know more about Big Spider-Bank than I know about Charlie Parker. In the first place, there's been infinitely more written about him. And he's been studied in much greater depth than Charlie Parker. However, I don't share, of course, the attitudes of many people about Charlie Parker's validity as an artist. And I would not have, as it were, made a study of him or his work as a result of that. I have listened extensively to Charlie Parker, both live and on records. I have studied the records, in fact, very carefully for extended periods of time just to find out if there was something I wasn't hearing that was in there. And while substantial originality is claimed for him, I never was able to discover it. And what is purported to be the jazz quality is something that I never have been able to find. And I never did know why anybody was interested in Charlie Parker as a musician, as an artist. This doesn't mean that there may be something I don't know that's happening. I have found that in many artists whose work I don't particularly enjoy, that I can nevertheless understand the basis of their appeals. But Charlie Parker, to that extent, eludes me entirely.
You don't understand the basis of his appeal?

Not at all. I don't know why anybody's interested in Charlie Parker. I could make a case for somebody being interested in Lester Young, which I'm not, but I can understand something of that. But I just can't understand it.

No, what happened with Charlie Parker is that, to a certain extent, he became a romantic hero of the beat generation. Oh, yes. Ferlinghetti, all the New York beat things. Now, the question as to why he did is somehow they read into his music a lot of protest themes. And, of course, you can take any musician's thing and read anything you wanted to it. But it's interesting that he became a kind of a basis for a romantic legend the same way Bix did. That is, in New York and Subway Walls, you'd have Bird Lives.

That's true. But as far as music is concerned, I mean, I can't understand the response of people to Mick Jagger or Alice Cooper and so on, because it is completely aesthetically meaningless to me. And I have worked with Charlie Parker and I have recorded Charlie Parker, and I have paid close and, I think, objective attention, or at least objective as much as I could be. And I found it certainly unexceptional.
It seems, Al, that socially and politically, we haven't really talked about your political views yet, but you say that you're a revolutionary socialist.
Yeah, I think that's a fair estimate.

And I'd like to ask you a little bit about that. But you tend to be, it seems that you tend to be extremely, I don't know whether the word radical would be correct, in your political views and extremely conservative in your views of music. That is, when all the figures musically that have been either used or in some way reflect a social change, these musicians don't appeal to you at all. The musicians that appeal to you are the ones that reflect a society that might have been slower, more static. I'm thinking of early 19th century New Orleans. That you're interested in the preservation of a true, what you call a true New Orleans form of music. And that you're not very interested in whether this music changes into another kind of form. In fact, you don't believe in any evolutionary views in this sense. Well, I believe that the jazz has gone through its process of evolution and died. All right. All right. But you're interested in that true form.
Oh, yes. Okay. Very much.

So that the question of how, what new musical form may arise on the horizon doesn't interest you very much right now, because it's all speculation or it's all, it doesn't, it just hasn't come into existence yet. That's right. But politically, you seem to be very interested in change taking place in the culture. And maybe, I just wonder how you roll out.

Of course, my political attitude is a classical one in this sense. And that is that I believe that any true revolutionary socialist maintains his position on an entirely defensive basis. That is, that he assumes that the capitalist society in which we live is in a process of decline and inevitable collapse. I see the basic conflict as it exists in the world as one between capital and labor, which is certainly classical. I believe that there comes a time in the relations between capital and labor against the economic political background and it is a system in which the capitalism can no longer afford the luxury of democracy and attempts to impose its and continue its system by force rather than by the machinery or the apparent, or the machinery of an apparent democratic process. Therefore, I consider that it is absolutely essential for working people to get themselves organized, to defend themselves against the onslaughts of the offense that they can anticipate from a capitalist class in decay, in exactly the same sense as I would have recommended it to the working class of Germany, as Hitler organized capitalism to oppress the working class, and as Franco did it in Spain, and as Mussolini did it in Italy. I consider that we're going to have to face the same kind of problems here at some time and worldwide. Therefore, there is no abstract ideological consideration involved. It's merely a question of trying to prepare for the inevitable collapse of the society that we have. Now, I never, I do not and never did believe that the arts serve only as propaganda tools for politics. I believe that there is such a thing as the happy life, and that man has experienced at various times and places the circumstances of a happy life, and that it is his job in order to satisfy himself to recreate those as much as possible. Now, it happens that, to me, that those things that occurred in our history, where this kind of life was apparent, was in New Orleans at the turn of the century, and certain other places like the Paris that produced the French Impressionists. And I'm for these things, and I enjoy them. And in the same way, I suppose that Coleridge enjoyed Xanadu, though he never lived there.
Now, New Orleans was a capitalist society at the turn of the century, or would you say?

Oh, yes, of course. All society at the turn of the century virtually was capitalist society, but it was capitalist society which was still in its ascendancy, and where the opportunities for the individual to make a life for himself still existed without the oppression of an oppressive economic system.

I just wonder, when you use the classic motto of capitalist labor, how you apply that to the American context, where you have a union, unionization of labor, which is so strong and conservative. It seems to me if the American people are going to be done in by anything, it's going to be George Meany as much as it is anybody else, and he represents the working class of America.

Well, as long as he continues to represent the working class of America, then the nation will not succumb to George Meany. The danger lies in that point where he decides for his own interest to make an alliance with the capitalists, that the danger exists.
Which has been done since the real history of American labor.

But what I'm saying is, as long as the working class itself understands its historic role, and even if it doesn't understand it, if it fights to defend its historic role, then it has a chance to survive. And we all, as a society, have a chance to survive.
But its historic role, at least in the American context, has been to get a slice of the capitalist pie.
That's right.
Which has always succeeded in doing.
My assumption is that the pie keeps getting smaller, and the time will come in the not-too-distant future when there's nothing left to slice.

Now, relating this back to the music again, do you see, then, the capitalist system as part of the American dream, which was valid at this point? Oh, yes, of course. Maybe until 1890s or something like that. Certainly.
The capitalist system, as it operated in America, still provided, certainly provided, an enormous amount of opportunity for individuals to be able to function independently.
Well, what do you see taking its place, then?

What do I see for the future? Well, it depends upon who's victorious in the struggle. I see a choice between fascism and socialism. Hmm. But I do not see a chance for the continuation of capitalism. Hmm. And as between fascism and socialism, I will choose the socialism.
What kind of socialism?

Because there are so many kinds. I just wondered what... There's only one kind of socialism, in fact. And that kind of socialism is a society that is organized in such a manner that the people that run the society have labor as their constituency. Hmm. Hmm. In other words, if you send a representative to Congress from a geographical district, he is basically responsible to represent the people in that district. In a socialist society, you would have a representative who came from the auto workers and a representative who came from the farm workers and so on. Hmm. That they would be represented by industry and that they would depend for their political lives upon the people that elected them, in fact. Hmm. Just as contemporary politicians are, except that the people would be different.
Hmm. Hmm.

Hmm. Hmm. Hmm. So, you don't depend in politics on goodwill or idealists. You depend... And also, you never try to come to political conclusions on the basis of moral judgments. And nothing is more futile than for anybody to talk about how things should be. It's necessary to see how things are and determine how you're going to deal with those processes. Certainly, I can't imagine anybody relishing the idea of a revolution in progress. But any more than I can see anybody looking forward to a gallbladder operation.
Hmm. Hmm.
But, in fact, there are certain things that are necessary, both in medicine and in life, which must be done for survival.
Certain things are inevitable, then. Yes. Now, this is going to occur through a natural process. It's not going to be a war for open warfare. Or...
Well, I can't see how it's going to be otherwise.
I mean, are you an orthodox Marxist in the sense you believe there's going to be an overthrow of a capitalist class?

Oh, yes. I can't imagine the American capitalist class or any capitalist class committing suicide as a class. I believe that the first job of every regime is to maintain itself in power. And I just can't see them peacefully surrendering it. However, I don't believe that it's going to succumb as a result of an onslaught from labor. I believe it is going to result as the failure of its own onslaught on labor. I can't see the working class taking the offensive or the initiative in creating a revolution. I can only see it as the... ...
